Engineering as a whole has some overlap with art, but just a tiny bit, and that's literally the part you describe to the AI. 90% of coding is akin to digging digital trenches or doing digital piping. Moving data from A to B or choosing how to store it or making sure there's no leak or corruption.

There is many games out there with character design or art that isn't clean or perfect, look at something like terraria for example. replies.author: luigi-mario-jr
replies.body:
Another programmer here, who has worked in web development, app development, game development, studied generative art, and has worked on one highly successful game project.

I agree completely that, game programming is (generally) art. I think it is very ignorant in how many “artists” gatekeep what they deem as art. There is a domain of programming literally called “generative art” (using code as a medium to produce art), but even with that obvious example put aside, there is so much nuance, care, and personal expression that needs to go into a game  such that a player can suspend disbelief that what they are seeing is not just images/sprites or 3d models moving on a screen. The interactions between all of the elements is most certainly important and not just a matter of “plumbing”. 

If someone treats game programming merely as plumbing or gluing libraries together, then I don’t believe they actually have what it takes to be a successful game programmer and should just stick to art. If writing words on a page can be considered art, and turning knobs on a synthesizer can be considered art, then game programming can absolutely and definitively be considered art. Anyone in the game development field who does not consider the code that makes Celeste move so gracefully as being art, is truly not seeing the complete picture.

What made celeste what it is isn't and will never be the  "I'm an artist" attitude of the author, it's the literal hundred of hours spent testing in practice the gameplay and tweaking it.

You could have made celeste with AI, it would have still taken hundred of hours of playtesting.

replies.author: Own_Manufacturer1188
replies.body:
Honestly, AI art often looks strange. It lacks the charm of the human art. I am not strictly against AI art, although I prefer to make my own assets. Coding is more “robotic” process. It’s logical and although it requires creativity, you can find a solution online most of the time. With actual art, such as music or drawing, it’s less logical, more about expressing yourself, which obviously AI can’t do. If you just need assets for a game and you don’t have a budget and/or time/skills to do it yourself, you can always resort for AI, since the final product is not the art, but the game as a whole. 

What I do have a problem with, however, are AI written posts that talk from a perspective of a real human. Say a gamedev vibecodes a game and then uses AI to write an article about his experience to promote the game. This loses any authenticity whatsoever in my opinion. It’s like leaving a machine to define your personality and review your memories to other people. Writing is also a form of art and I personally hate AI written texts - it sounds all the same.

Because art is not really art when it reuses someone else’s work and just combines it together. Coding is different, you often reuse existing snippets of code you find on Stack Overflow etc. It’s always been like that. Art cannot be machine-learned. It’s just someone else’s style and imagination. In programming, you only have a limited number of solutions for existing problems and the program itself is the product. If you used AI to create brushes, mix colours for you and set your program up, it’s more comparable to AI writing code imho. You are free to disagree with me if you’d like to, this is just my two cents.

For context, I have both artistic and coding background experience, despite me not being somehow exceptionally good in neither of those. replies.author: Own_Manufacturer1188
replies.body:
The value of actual art is in the technique and expression that comes from within. When I ask AI to create art, it does so, and I might like it, but is it really my own expression? You see, when you imagine a cool knight in armor with a sword, you probably have a more or less specific vision, but the execution will not be yours. I could show you 10 different knight guys and if it fits the style (say, gothic medieval fantasy), then you’ll most likely be satisfied with those pictures. If you had to draw it yourself and had the skills to do so, I guarantee you it would have looked different. The style would be authentic, and there would be an actually creative thought behind each brush stroke/pencil line. This is what makes art be art. AI can create **assets**, but that’s not art from my definition, despite it coming from your idea. 

Again, I can respect other people’s opinions, and I don’t really see a point in arguing any further. If you believe AI art is actual art, you do you. I just think this is not something AI should be dominant in, because in time, the creativity will vanish and all that’ll be left is just strange, similar looking slop.

replies.author: Own_Manufacturer1188
replies.body:
AI is incapable of actually creating stuff, although it seems wild. Everything AI generates is just mesh of stuff made by other people. That’s why all AI art looks similar. It’s why when you see an AI ad on YouTube, it looks uncanny. The person looks familiar, but isn’t at the same time. When a human creates art, it’s authentic. You may look around for reference objects, but at the same time you use your actual fantasy to do stuff. AI specifically takes existing stuff and mixes it together. No matter how realistic or stylized it is, it’s always gonna be different. 

An example that comes to mind is animation. When you have stuff like Arcane, created by humans with actual depth, insanely complex and beautiful details, with faces that actually carry believable emotions, AI could never do such thing. If it creates something similar, it’s because it literally just copies it and maybe applies it on a different picture, like a reference photo or something. That’s, in my honest opinion, not art. 

Same goes for writing. We have, as a humanity, come to a point where writing becomes something done by AI. But could AI ever create a story from scratch? Would it be able to create LOTR if Tolkien was never alive? I would say that’s highly unlikely, or rather straight up impossible. What it can do is to analyze Tolkien’s existing work and replicate it, or apple that style to another text, but it couldn’t create it on its own. And that’s my whole point. 

If you need assets for your game and your game is the product, then AI is okay-ish (I still prefer to make it myself, but that’s besides the point). If you want to create an art exhibition, I don’t see AI fit to create the art for you, unless it’s some extravagant experiment. If you want to create art and use AI to do it, it’s just not it for me. If you need art assets to create a good game, then I believe it’s justifiable. As I said, you don’t have to agree with me, it’s just my own opinion.

replies.author: da_blue_jester
replies.body:
You could argue that AI code is no different to Stackoverlow copy and pasting. We've all been guilty of that - but then figuring out what the code does AFTER your solution works is the education piece. In my humble opinion I don't think AI Coded games are all that big an issue. You can spend a few hours writing the functions and plumbing up the signals (spot the Godot developer) or you can write the technical task and have Claude do it in a few minutes while you spend time then on the art or some other task. 

I think the line being drawn with Art is that AI is stealing the art from other sources to make the thing for people. Now if you used AI to make an animation tool and you supplied the first image yourself that would be different because then it's a tool assist, but just going 'Make me a space marine style gun' it pulls from other existing artwork and that's the 'gripe' others have. At least that's my read on it. 

That being said I enjoy coding, I don't want to fully give it over. It's like writing a book or composing music, there is an art to it and we all have clear styles. But if I get stuck on a feature that I can't debug I also know that i wouldn't mind using a tool to help me get it solved. If that tool is a Google search or an AI what's the difference in the end. What we should want to avoid is one-prompt games that nobody tests first and just fires up.

If you're telling those interns what to write and where, how to structure it and making sure it complies with rules like, "dont declare everything as global variables" and "organize your presentation vs data layers" along with "here's how the classes should look, here's how the functions should be defined", then sure, it's real "we did it ourselves programming" because you are architecting a solution rather than having your intern do the solution for you.

It does write very good. I've been coding most of my life and I've completely handed over the reigns to it. What it won't do is the larger architectural decisions on it's own. That's where you still have to come in. It'll match the scope and expectations you set for it. If you have a large scope system but feed it nothing but small tasks you're going to run into some issues down the road.

Here's an example where I screwed up with AI.

I'm working on a game now for a while now. It plays a very particular way. There's segments that were layered onto the game that break from the original convention of the game. I'm having a really difficult time now getting claude to get this right. It's getting there but because I didn't plan around that from the start it's feeling a bit janky. I'm still plugging away at it but spending a huge amount of time in the planning stages pays off down the road.

This is why  I still like to use an IDE to see files of code when I want to  but one that allows me to harness ai agents to help with the flow of work and create its own documents in main editor pane that are immersive and interactive. . It just allows me to do more. AI has made art components really cheap to create and AI can now brush stroke in blender so is this still AI art if the user is looking and telling AI what he wants the end result to look like AI. The first think I did was criteria persona as a marine biologist, gave it [skills.sh](http://skills.sh) af a researcher and had hime do the research and be in charge of the actual realism of the fishing game. What fish one can find in what lake. The wole concept was to have a group of specilized agents with a seperation from builder to auditor in an orchestrated enabled enviroment.

Workflows such as asking a Codex to use imagen to create sides, front back views and using tripo for 3d modeling and then using Codex again to fix small errors in blender.

Different personas get different responsibilities. All agents across platform can communicate and are connected to an mcp central system and a system projected coherency state of who I am and what do I do and when am I now and how am I working with and what is my role.

I try to give them as many tools as possible. Access to elevenlab for sounds, to dreamina for clips. Codex does the storyboard with imagen and when I am satisfied, he creates the clips.

comments.author: KeeperofAbyss
comments.body:
Finally a success story everyone has been asking for 

There are key components to it - be transparent to audience, know what you are doing, plan well, refine and most importantly make a game you would like to play

It is so easy to lose track from your project especially with AI.

Currently working on a game and I have co-worker who works on their game. We both use AI and constantly exchange highlights, how we approached feature design, what worked, what didn't and we share tips so we don't step into same bucket etc.

Yes it is easy to do a game clone in 1-3 prompts. But it is not easy to create something original or even keep adding original content into existing clone.

Also tip - use Godot and write custom plugins, helps maintaining your game a lot

comments.author: kawai777

Terms like “slop” and “vibe coding” are reductive and intellectually misleading.
Disclosing the use of AI/SI should promote transparency, not invite prejudice or discrimination.
Intellectual rigor demands precise terminology and objective technical evaluation.
Criticize the implementation, demonstrate its defects, and substantiate your claims.
A label is not an argument, and disclosure is not an admission of inferiority.

comments.author: kawai777
comments.body: Before arguing on "AI art" and "AI art slop", should we not establish what art is? Is the prompt the object's material, the intention of its creation, or, is it an instruction to an instrument? If a man creates a prompt, is the instrument an extension of his artistic mind? If a person creates it, how does the art not belong to the individual? If a machine creates a prompt, how much of the art's origin is human? Is the soul of art that of the author, of the creation, or of the spectator? Does the author have to be conscious? Before denouncing the product of its author, shouldn't we first establish what the content of an art piece makes it?
